notes:
I've put together notes on Ecclesiastes 8, covering all 17 verses, but several of the sources you named are missing. I couldn't open enduringword.com, and I found nothing from the Catholic or Orthodox sites or from any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Catholic voices appear only second-hand: the Pulpit Commentary quotes Gregory the Great and the Latin Vulgate. NET Bible notes appear only where preceptaustin.org quotes them. On denominations, the sources mostly disagree on how to read the text, not along church lines. So I name each commentator and give a tradition only where your site list or the page itself gives one.

**v. 1**
- The usual reading: the truly wise person is rare. Wisdom shows in the face, making a hard face gentle and humble. Wesley (wesley.nnu.edu, which you list as Methodist) says wisdom makes a man venerable, chearful, mild, and amiable and that the face is put for the mind, because the mind discovers itself in the countenance. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
- Gill reports the Jewish Aramaic paraphrase (the Targum), which applies "interpretation" to understanding the prophets. Gill widens it to explaining God's works and word, and to teaching others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/8-1.htm
- Ryken's reading via preceptaustin: Daniel is the example. Godly wisdom becomes more gracious, merciful, and forgiving, and the verse links to Proverbs 15:13. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-8-commentary
- Where it belongs is debated. Keil & Delitzsch report that Luther and others regard Ecclesiastes 8:1 as of the nature of an epilogue to what goes before, but they disagree with him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/8-1.htm Michael Eaton (via preceptaustin) also attaches it to chapter 7. Glenn instead sees v. 1 (wisdom's value) and v. 17 (wisdom's limits) as bookends of the chapter. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-8-commentary
- Ancient translations: the Greek Septuagint reads "a man shameless in countenance will be hated." The Latin Vulgate reads "the Almighty will change his face." The Pulpit Commentary thinks neither follows the Hebrew accurately. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/8-1.htm

**v. 2**
- The usual reading: keep your oath of loyalty made before God. Constable says the wise man keeps his oath of allegiance that he has made before God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-8.html
- Pulpit Commentary: this is a religious duty as well as good sense. It may lie behind Paul's Romans 13. The "oath of God" is a loyalty oath sworn in God's name. Pulpit rejects the idea that "king" here means God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html
- Different reading of the oath: Wesley takes it as that oath which thou hast taken to keep all God's laws, whereof this of obedience to superiors is one. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/ Translations also differ: the ESV has "because of God's oath to him." https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-8-commentary
- Preceptaustin's own comment: the verse is not about absolute loyalty, but about honoring God's order in a fallen world with wise, godly discretion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-8-commentary

**v. 3**
- Barrick: don't leave hastily; wait for the king to dismiss you, and avoid anything that would displease him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-8-commentary
- Wesley reads it as don't withdraw from the king's service in discontent, and if you have offended him, don't persist. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/ Clarke: if you are in the wrong, don't try to defend yourself, because his power is absolute. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ecclesiastes-8.html
- Pulpit Commentary takes the "evil thing" as a conspiracy or uprising. It notes the clause is ambiguous, and some read it as "obey not a sinful command." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html

**v. 4**
- Pulpit Commentary: the king's word is all-powerful. Job 9:12 and Isaiah 45:9 use the same "what are you doing?" language of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html
- Constable: the wise man does not dispute the king's authority and sovereignty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-8.html

**v. 5**
- Pulpit Commentary: the context shows the commandment is the king's, not God's. Obedience need not be servile, and cases like Daniel's, where obeying would be sin, aren't in view. The wise man waits patiently because he knows a judgment is coming. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html
- Wesley differs: he says Solomon passes to a new subject, the wise discerning when and how to keep God's commands. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
- Matthew Henry points to Esther with Ahasuerus as an example of discerning time and manner. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Ecc/Ecc_008.cfm Clarke breaks it into when, how and what. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ecclesiastes-8.html
- On the limits of obedience: Coffman points to the three Hebrew young men and to Daniel, who defied royal orders. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/ecclesiastes-8.html Bridgeway reads it as acting without disobeying the king neither do they sin against their conscience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ecclesiastes/8-8.html

**v. 6**
- Barrick: this repeats Ecclesiastes 3:1, a time for every matter. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-8-commentary
- Whose misery? Pulpit Commentary prefers the tyrant's own wickedness, which will bring him down. The other reading is the subjects' suffering, which calls for God to step in. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html Wesley: the right way and time are known to God but mostly hidden from people, so most people bring misery on themselves. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/

**v. 7**
- Wesley: people don't know the future, so their minds are uneasy. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/ Pulpit Commentary suggests the person in view may be the tyrant, who can't see his downfall coming. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html
- A devotional note on biblehub: the uncertainty should lead to trust in God, not despair. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/ecclesiastes/8.htm

**v. 8**
- "Wind" or "breath/spirit"? Pulpit Commentary prefers "wind" (compare John 3:8). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say "breath of life," Not "wind," as WEISS thinks. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Ecc/Ecc_008.cfm
- "No discharge": Matthew Henry and Wesley take it as the losing battle with death. Wesley adds that the most subtle wickedness cannot outwit death. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/ Pulpit Commentary compares strict Persian military service, which allowed no exemptions. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html
- Constable (labelled on the page as non-denominational, dispensational): no one escapes the results of his own wickedness, because the king will punish. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ecclesiastes/8-8.html Barrick reads four illustrations of human powerlessness, the last literally "wickedness will not deliver its masters." https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-8-commentary
- A preacher's application: the Biblical Illustrator uses "no discharge" for the Christian's lifelong service. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ecclesiastes-8.html

**v. 9**
- Whose hurt? Wesley says the tyrant's own, as he brings God's vengeance on himself. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/ Clarke agrees. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ecclesiastes-8.html Pulpit Commentary says most modern commentators mean the oppressed subject, though it may be deliberately ambiguous. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html

**v. 10** (the most disputed verse)
- Wording: the ESV footnote says most Hebrew manuscripts read "forgotten," while some Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint and the Vulgate read "praised." https://www.blueletterbible.org/esv/ecc/8/12/
- Who is the verse about?
  - Keil & Delitzsch: the wicked are buried in peace, while those who acted rightly had to leave the holy place and were forgotten. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/8-10.htm Constable likewise sees two unfair outcomes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-8.html
  - Pulpit Commentary disagrees: the whole verse is about the wicked man, whose evil is forgotten in the very city where he did it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html
  - The Geneva Study Bible takes those who left the holy place to be people who feared God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/8-10.htm
- What is "the holy place"?
  - Wesley: the throne or court of justice of wicked rulers. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
  - Spurgeon (spurgeon.org is one of your Baptist sites; this sermon is on studylight): the judgment-seat the place where the magistrate dispenses justice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ecclesiastes/8-10.html
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown mention Joab, whom Solomon had taken from the temple and killed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Ecc/Ecc_008.cfm
- Catholic line (through the Vulgate's "praised as men of just works"): Pulpit Commentary quotes Gregory the Great applying the verse to hypocrites hidden in a peaceful Church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html

**v. 11**
- All the sources agree: people mistake God's patience for indifference. Clarke: patience meant to lead to repentance is abused to lead to more crimes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ecclesiastes-8.html Henry: Vengeance comes slowly, but it comes surely. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Ecc/Ecc_008.cfm
- MacArthur (gty.org, Baptist list) via preceptaustin: the delay doesn't lessen the certainty of final judgment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-8-commentary
- Chuck Smith links it to 2 Peter 3 and scoffing at Christ's return. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/ecclesiastes-8.html

**vv. 12–13**
- Preceptaustin: the turn from puzzlement to confidence, like Psalm 73. The writer drops his usual "I have seen"; this truth he knows by conviction and holds by faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-8-commentary
- The apparent clash (the sinner lives long in v. 12, but his days don't lengthen in v. 13): Kidner (via preceptaustin) suggests v. 13 hints at hope after death for the godly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-8-commentary Wesley: the wicked man's life is but a shadow, which will quickly vanish. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/

**v. 14**
- Wesley: the injustice comes either from wicked rulers or from God's providence, for weighty reasons. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/ Henry: blame the world for its emptiness, not God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Ecc/Ecc_008.cfm
- Coffman is critical of Solomon here, citing Abel and Cain to show that the Torah already taught this. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/ecclesiastes-8.html

**v. 15** (a real split)
- Godly enjoyment (majority view):
  - Barnes: the verse is unfairly charged with Epicureanism; pleasure is God's gift, received with thanks. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/8-15.htm
  - Gill: contentment and cheerfulness, not a pleasure-seeker's creed. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/ecclesiastes/8-15.html
  - Constable: not in a pleasure-mad way. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-8.html
  - GotQuestions: the verse is like 1 Timothy 6:8, and the rich fool in Luke 12 twists it. https://www.gotquestions.org/eat-drink-and-be-merry.html
- Earthly or sensual voice:
  - Poole gives both options: spoken as a sensual man, or in Solomon's own voice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/8-15.htm
  - Wesley's note is short: This he speaks of sensual delights. His introduction says the book is partly dramatic, voicing ungodly men at times. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
  - Coffman calls it Solomon's version of Epicurean thinking. Smith calls it human philosophy and human reasoning. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ecclesiastes/8-15.html
- Gill reports that the Targum reads it as the joy of the law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/8-15.htm

**vv. 16–17**
- Even the wisest, hardest-working person can't fully understand God's ways. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-8.html
- Wesley: so don't wear yourself out asking; submit quietly to God's providence. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
- Barrick: even the wisest is a fool compared with God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-8-commentary Pulpit Commentary says the section really runs on into chapter 9. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-8.html
